# Player Animation Authoring and Builds

## Source and Generated Files

| File or directory | Purpose | Maintenance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `player_movement.bbmodel` | Editable project containing the skeleton, reference model, and twenty animations | Edit and save in Blockbench |
| `project.json` | Source-project list, namespaces, bone bindings, and coordinate conventions | Update when changing the binding contract |
| `platforms/<platform>/build/shared/common/generated/animation-resources/` | JSON resources loaded by the game | Generated by Gradle; do not edit manually |
| `platforms/<platform>/build/shared/common/reports/animations/export.json` | Source/output SHA-256 hashes, output manifest, and format version | Generated by the exporter |
| `tools/animation-exporter/` | Build-time Java exporter | Maintain with the animation contract and tests |
| `common/src/test/resources/animation/initial_p0/` | Independent regression fixtures for the original prototypes | Migration tests only; not runtime resources or sources for further animation edits |

The `.bbmodel` project is the sole maintained source of action keyframes. Java defines rig dimensions, interpolation, and mesh deformation as playback contracts; individual action keyframes belong in the source project.

The bullet jump's ROOT Y rotation describes an axial spin in launch coordinates. Runtime orientation aligns the whole pose with launch yaw/pitch. `project.json` declares this action as `launch` in `coordinate_spaces`; undeclared actions use `entity` coordinates. Direction and keyframed pose layers have separate transitions. Real bullet jumps and local previews use the same animation resource; previews do not apply movement impulses.

## Editing Workflow

1. Open `player_movement.bbmodel` in Blockbench 5.x. It uses the native Free Model format and needs no GeckoLib plugin.
2. Switch to Animate and select an action, such as `slide`, `bullet_jump`, `crouch_idle`, `crouch_walk`, `roll`, `roll_left`, `roll_right`, or `roll_backward`.
3. Edit translations and rotations on the upper arms, thighs, and other bones. Use the **X rotation** of `left_forearm`, `right_forearm`, `left_shin`, and `right_shin` to adjust elbows and knees.
4. Choose linear, step, or Bezier interpolation. Bezier time and value handles are preserved during export.
5. Save the `.bbmodel` file and run `gradlew generateAnimations` to inspect the export, or run `gradlew build`.
6. Run `gradlew check` to verify the math, resource contract, and exporter, then preview the result in-game.

Normal builds need Gradle and the configured Java toolchain. They do not require Blockbench, Python, MCP, or UI automation. The build runs `generateAnimations → processResources → jar`. Exported animation names do not require Java registration.

Add source projects through `projects` in `project.json`. Animation names become resource paths under their project's namespace. Names may contain lowercase letters, digits, underscores, hyphens, and directory separators, for example `motion/air_turn`. Output IDs must be unique across all source projects.

## Rig and Coordinate Contract

- Blockbench uses upward Y, model-pixel translations, degrees, seconds, and ZYX Euler order.
- Runtime coordinates use downward Y, model-pixel translations, radians, and seconds.
- Translation converts to `[x, -y, z]`. Rotation converts to `[-x, y, -z]`, then to radians. Full turns retain their continuous angles.
- The torso rotates around the hips. The head and upper arms inherit the torso pose; thighs inherit the overall pose.
- Explicit bindings map forearm and shin control bones to limb `bend` channels, limited to ±120 degrees.
- `HumanoidRig` defines the runtime bind pose and hierarchy for `humanoid_v1`. Export validates the source project, manifest, and runtime contract together. Renaming a source bone requires updating its manifest binding.
- The reference model uses standard-width arms. Runtime standing offsets account for standard and slim player skins; verify both models visually when editing poses.

Source cubes and the original reference texture are authoring aids. They are not exported as a replacement player model or skin. Editing reference geometry does not change the player's collision box. Bind-pose changes or additional movable axes require a rig-contract update and runtime adaptation.

## Curves and Compatibility

Runtime resources use internal format **v3**, including the action coordinate space, per-keyframe interpolation, and Bezier handles. The reader retains compatibility with v1 numeric tracks and v2 Bezier resources. In v3, `coordinate_space` must explicitly be `entity` or `launch`.

Step interpolation takes precedence over neighboring Bezier handles. Bezier curves are evaluated by time, and rotation tracks retain continuous angles. If a source keyframe omits handles, the exporter uses Blockbench's native ±0.1-second time handles with zero value offsets, including transitions between linear and Bezier keyframes.

Supported data includes numeric position, Euler rotation, elbow/knee X controls, one-shot and looping playback, and linear/step/Bezier interpolation. Every track needs a keyframe at time zero. Nonconstant looping tracks also need a keyframe at the end of the animation.

Unsupported features fail the build with the source project and reason: Catmull-Rom interpolation, Molang expressions, scale, global rotation, quaternion track interpolation, IK, effect tracks, separate pre/post keyframe values, delay expressions, and Hold playback. Unsupported data must not be silently discarded.

See Blockbench's [native animation semantics](https://github.com/JannisX11/blockbench/blob/master/js/animations/timeline_animators.js) and [Bezier handle definitions](https://github.com/JannisX11/blockbench/blob/master/js/animations/keyframe.js). Runtime root-finding for Bezier time curves can differ slightly from the editor viewport's discrete curve sampling.

## Previews and In-Game Validation

Blockbench displays elbow and knee poses with segmented bones. The game uses continuous mesh curvature, so joint surfaces, wrist positions, and bounds need not match the rigid editor segments point for point. Automated tests constrain keyframes and coordinate conversion; inspect skins, armor, held items, intersections, and action transitions in-game.

UI automation is optional for operating the editor or game, not a resource-production or build dependency. Keep editor inspection, automated results, and gameplay validation separate.

Local preview commands provide resource-ID completion:

```text
/nfp animation play ninjas_free_play:slide_to_bullet_jump
/nfp animation sample ninjas_free_play:slide 0.5
/nfp animation view 90
/nfp animation aim -45
/nfp animation aim reset
/nfp animation stop
```

`play` starts an animation, `sample` holds a pose at a given time in seconds, and `view` rotates the preview model for inspection. `aim` simulates launch pitch, with negative values pointing upward; `aim reset` restores camera-pitch input. `aim` also updates a held pose's orientation. `stop` ends the preview.

Previews do not activate physical movement or synchronize preview actions to the server. Inspect the model in third person. Restart the development instance after changing resource-format or player code; compatible runtime-resource edits can use a resource reload.

To repeatedly interrupt two separate actions:

```text
/nfp animation chain ninjas_free_play:slide ninjas_free_play:bullet_jump 0.6
```

`chain` alternates actions at the specified interval until `stop`, a new `play`/`sample`, a resource reload, or world exit. The minimum interval is one tick. Switching happens on client ticks and exercises real playback interruption, rather than a combined action authored on a single timeline.

### Crouch and Roll Checks

`crouch_idle` and `crouch_walk` are asymmetric low-stance loops. The front knee is roughly at a right angle, the rear knee points forward above the ground, and the torso rises 37.5 degrees above the ground. The head remains attached to the neck. Arms spread slightly to the sides with natural elbow bends; hands sit horizontally ahead of the player's feet, rather than along the tilted torso's local forward axis, without forming an embracing silhouette.

The visual silhouette can extend above the default half-height collision box. Check low ceilings separately. Compare feet, elbows, and palms across horizontal orientations and the full gait: a palm ahead of the feet does not establish that the forearm bends forward. Each palm must also be ahead of its elbow. Check the entire forearm against the armored torso, excluding the normal shoulder attachment region.

`roll` progresses through a forward dive, chin tuck, shoulder/back contact, and recovery. Arms and legs retain extension and separation; the dive preserves ground clearance until the shoulder/back can contact the ground. Its visual height may exceed one block instead of compressing every joint into the half-height collider. Side flips and backward handsprings use natural rig height rather than uniform half-height scaling. Roll poses disable the head's world-aim override and preserve authored head motion.

Roll duration proportionally retimes source animation and Bezier time handles while preserving phase and full rotations. Only crouches and forward rolls use half-height reference adaptation. Hand-support timing comes from the three JSON resources in `common/src/main/resources/assets/ninjas_free_play/ninja_contacts/`, interpolated by normalized phase. Ground queries and bounded contact locking affect rendering, not entity position.

Edit `.bbmodel` files to change silhouettes, gaits, or rotation timing, not generated animation JSON. Optional contact baking and offline inspection are covered in the [authoring tools guide](../tools/animation-authoring/README.md).

### Parkour and Equipment

The source contains twenty actions. Parkour clips include `aim_glide`, `wall_latch`, `wall_dash`, `air_flip`, and `flying_kick`, plus six directional variants: `wall_dash_left`, `wall_dash_right`, `wall_dash_away`, `wall_latch_left`, `wall_latch_back`, and `wall_latch_right`.

Animations preserve right-click item use. Hand adaptation follows the item action; eating and drinking retain the source body pose, and bow/shield aiming preserves overall tilt. Wall-latch foot endpoints use the actual support plane, including standard skin overlays and boot expansion. ROOT corrections use continuous entry and exit responses.

Flying-kick direction comes from the final straight-leg axis in the source pose, then aligns with the movement vector. Physical movement code must not contain copied keyframe angles. Validate new poses with both arm widths, skin overlays, standard armor, both hands, bows, shields, and food.

## Transition Algorithm and Tuning

Action keyframes and Bezier handles live in Blockbench. `AnimationPlayer` and `PoseTransition` manage transitions between actions. Switching estimates incoming/outgoing velocities at a fixed `0.0001`-second sample interval, capturing position, Euler-angle, and bend differences and velocity differences for every bone. A cubic Hermite correction decays to zero and joins the target track's velocity. Repeated interruption rebuilds this correction instead of retaining a recursive blend tree.

Weights preserve their derivative at the switch. Curve control values remain in `[0, 1]`, shortening the transition when necessary. Stopping continues sampling the outgoing action while fading it out. One-shot actions continue from their endpoint velocity and decelerate rather than freezing limbs immediately. Held poses use a constant animation source and share the same playback/stop mechanism; selecting a sample time is an intentional direct seek.

ROOT rotation retains full turns instead of choosing a new principal interval each frame. Equivalent whole turns are removed at fade-out start only when the action weight is one, avoiding a reverse full-turn motion during the fade. Commands use a render clock with partial ticks; alternating previews use a tick clock so command transitions do not jump back to integer-tick time.

Client `Animation.Transition_Seconds` defaults to `0.15` seconds, with a `0–1` range; zero cuts immediately. Adjust action timing and handles before changing transition duration. Loop endpoints need matching position and tangents; rotations may differ by an equivalent full turn. The player does not rewrite authored steps, corners, or unclosed loops. At the ±120-degree elbow/knee limit, joint constraints take priority over velocity continuity.

Regression coverage includes pose and velocity on both sides of an interruption, stopping/resuming during fade-in, full-turn principal boundaries, endpoint and stop-angle relocation, 1,000 consecutive interruptions, different render sampling rates, and pairwise transitions. Numerical continuity does not establish freedom from intersections, skin stretching, or poor silhouettes; inspect these visually.

## Optional MCP Editing

The source project can be round-tripped through the local `blockbench-mcp` document engine and saved natively by Blockbench. Point authoring tools at a local checkout with `--mcp-root`; MCP is not a mod build dependency.

Document round trips must preserve Bezier handles, linking flags, and keyframe precision. `keyframe_add`, `keyframes_add_bulk`, and `keyframe_list` pass this metadata through `extra_fields`. Restart the MCP process after updating its implementation. This document support does not establish equivalent Bezier support in its Bedrock or GeckoLib exporters; this project uses its own Java exporter to read native `.bbmodel` files.

## Pose and Runtime Constraints

- **Wall latch:** `wall_latch`, `wall_latch_left`, `wall_latch_back`, and `wall_latch_right` define front, side, and back poses. View-sector blending is continuous without restarting the loop. Torso, head, and legs move together; feet rotate about the hips to meet the wall without translating joints apart. Relative quaternion error smoothing avoids a reverse sweep at the 180-degree back-facing boundary.
- **Wall dash:** upward reach/pull, lateral reach/pull, and outward two-handed push gestures are source keyframes. The direction layer follows the view smoothly. Reachable wall surfaces align hand/foot endpoints; contact corrections smooth independently and fade out when interrupted.
- **Aim glide:** the source supplies a roughly 45-degree balanced pose, with the right hand forward, left hand back-left, and legs separated. Runtime tilt is `30 + 30 * 2^(-v/8)` degrees, where `v` is three-dimensional speed in blocks per second. Horizontal body facing follows motion and retains its last direction at rest. Eating/drinking adapt only the active hand to the head-relative mouth target; the other hand balances. Other item aiming twists around the existing torso axis while preserving tilt.
- **Flying kick:** a one-second one-shot action prepares during `0–0.09` seconds, extends and turns onto the right side during `0.09–0.18`, then holds. Side tilt rises from about 40 to 65 degrees. After extension, torso and striking-leg axes differ by about 5 degrees; the body aligns with travel, foot leading and head behind, right shoulder lowered and chest facing sideways. The other knee stays moderately tucked, arms balance naturally, and the head looks forward from the side. The striking foot leads both hands and the other foot. Direction uses the final foot axis, not the initial tucked pose.
- **Slide:** the extended leg is about 30 degrees above the ground, the torso about 60 degrees, and the acute angle between them about 30 degrees. Visual geometry is independent of the axis-aligned collision box; inspect low ceilings and equipment separately.
- **Backward handspring:** spread the legs and arms while airborne and retain sufficient support height during hand contact. After changing keyframes, rebake only the selected action's ROOT contact track.

Source-geometry tests cover pairwise interruptions, four-way latch foot/hip constraints, eating/drinking hands, torso aiming axes, and continuous contact release. They do not replace in-game equipment and intersection checks.

The independent glide layer preserves roll and flying-kick animations. Beginning a glide during a bullet jump ends the bullet-jump action and transitions to the glide pose; releasing right-click does not restore the old clip. This behavior comes from the movement controller, not render priority alone. Movement synchronization carries the auxiliary layer separately from the main action, including the shared slide-boost baseline and validation of predicted entry speeds.

The kick's toe direction depends on the parent hierarchy, thigh rotation, and shin bend. Changes to the tuck curve need compensating thigh rotation so the terminal shin axis retains its direction throughout extension. `KickExtensionTest` checks rapid forward extension, bent-to-straight knee motion, no late retraction, toe alignment across yaw/pitch, right-shoulder-down orientation around horizontal headings, head range, and the attacking silhouette. `ParkourStyleTest` checks torso/striking-leg alignment and the other leg's moderate bend. Keep this action one-shot; a loop must not repeat the tuck.
